title: Karaikkal Ammaiyar and the dance of bliss
hookLine: a saint climbs Shiva's mountain without setting foot on it and asks only to watch him dance; Nataraja's calm face, and why Hindus go for darshan
carry: darshan: to see god and be seen
tomorrow: where did the sounds of Sanskrit come from?

lines: UP THE MOUNTAIN, FEET NEVER TOUCHING.
cards: A woman climbs a holy mountain without once setting her feet on it; it's Shiva's home, and she goes up upside down.
She is thin as a skeleton, by her own prayer: when her husband grew afraid of her devotion and left, she asked Shiva to take her beauty away. Now she's coming to Kailash.
And when Shiva sees her, the story says, he turns to Parvati and says: here comes our mother. Her name is Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother from Karaikkal, and she has one thing to ask.

teach.h: SHE ASKS TO WATCH HIM DANCE.
teach.b: In the Periya Puranam, the Tamil lives of Shiva's saints, Shiva asks what she wants.
In the telling, she asks not to be born again; if she must be, never to forget him; and above all, to sit at his feet and sing while he dances.

He sends her south, to Tiruvalangadu, where tradition says she watches his dance forever. Her poems are among the oldest songs to Shiva the dancer, and old bronzes show her small and bony at his feet, singing.
So look at what she wanted to see.
Nataraja: nata, dancer, raja, king. The king of dancers. Arms swinging, hair flying, a ring of fire, one leg kicked high.
And in the middle of all that motion, the face: calm, sometimes with the faintest smile.
The dance is called the ananda tandava, the dance of bliss. Many Hindus read it as God moving the whole world without strain.

teach.h: DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.
teach.b: And here's the practice it explains: darshan, seeing. When the curtain opens at a temple, people press forward not to hear a speech but to see God, and to be seen.
The mother of Karaikkal gave up beauty, home and husband, and asked for darshan forever. Most of what a screen shows you is looking for your attention.
Darshan turns that around: you look at the face that is already looking at you, kindly.

how: Images of Shiva as Nataraja stand in many Shiva temples, especially in Tamil Nadu, where bronzes are bathed, dressed and carried in processions, and devotees come for darshan; Karaikkal Ammaiyar is honored among the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva.

o: a dance step taught to temple dancers in South India
Shiva as king of dancers, seen through a saint's eyes
a warrior god who fights demons with four weapons

games.q: the saint and the dancer — tap the pairs.
p: asked to watch him dance forever

s: Karaikkal Ammaiyar asked Shiva for beauty and riches
she asked to lose her beauty, and to sit at his feet singing while he dances.
Nataraja's face strains with the effort of the dance
everything else moves; the face is calm, sometimes with the faintest smile.
at darshan, people come to see God and to be seen
seeing the deity's face is at the heart of Hindu temple worship.

games.q: you're the mother of Karaikkal, and Shiva asks what you want. by the Periya Puranam's telling, what do you ask?
o: a palace on Kailash, near him.
to sit at his feet and sing while he dances.
your beauty back, and your husband home.
games.why: she asks for darshan forever: to sit at his feet and sing while he dances. he sends her to Tiruvalangadu.

practice: If you have an image of God at home, a picture or a murti, rest your eyes on its face for a few slow breaths, the way people stand at darshan. If you don't pray, look at something living instead, a plant, a tree, the sky.
Let your own face go quiet like the dancer's: forehead smooth, jaw loose, eyes soft. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, as you look.

wordCard.voice: Nataraja explained. Nataraja is the king of dancers, Shiva as lord of the dance, seen today through the eyes of the saint who asked to watch him forever.

orig.note: Sanskrit: darshana, seeing; at the temple, seeing God and being seen.

carryVoice: Your line: darshan, to see God and be seen. The mother of Karaikkal asked for nothing more. That's today, done.
